newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai ministers review IMF package.
newsitem.headline: Thai ministers review IMF package.

text.p: Thailand's economic ministers met on Monday to discuss a package of measures worked out with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to heal the ailing economy, a government spokeswoman said.
The package, which could include a standby credit facility or other aid from the IMF, is due to be presented to the cabinet on Tuesday.
The spokeswoman said the government would hold a news conference after the ministers' meeting around midday (0500 GMT) on Monday but gave no further details.

Japanese financial newspaper Nihon Keizai Shimbun said on Sunday the Export-Import Bank of Japan and the IMF have put together an $8 billion emergency loan package for Thailand to help boost the beleaguered economy.
Japan's private banks would coordinate several billion dollars in additional loans to help Bangkok shore up its foreign reserves and restructure its economy, the Nihon Keizai Shimbun said.
The report was not confirmed by Thai officials who said details would be released on Tuesday.

The newspaper said the plan would be unveiled by the EXIM after Tuesday when the government officially unveils the restructuring plan, which is expected to meet IMF lending conditions and include a request for loans from Japan.

Finance ministry sources said the conditions prescribed by the IMF would include further large cuts to the government budget, a value-added tax increase, a high interest rate policy at least until the end of this year and a reduction of the government's risk exposure to the troubled finance and property sectors.
They said if these conditions were met, Thailand would have access to the IMF's facilities.

Thailand is facing its worst economic crisis in decades following a prolonged economic boom which saw heavy overseas borrowing and misallocation of resources to non-productive areas such as the property sector.
Its financial institutions have been hit hard by a liquidity crunch and rising non-performing loans.

Thailand's foreign currency debt now totals almost $90 billion, about three-quarters of which is to the private sector. Nearly $40 billion of that debt is short-term and comes due before the end of the year.

Analysts have said there are concerns in the government that creditors may not roll over debt due to a lack of confidence in the government's ability to implement tough enough measures to boost the economy.
Bankers from of 25 foreign financial institutions met Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh on Sunday to express concerns over their debt exposure.
Chavalit said he had reassured them that they would be treated fairly.
Participants in the meeting said Chavalit asked them to cooperate by extending credit lines and rolling over loans to Thai companies.
